findings.text: The site's address is doodla.github.io/athena/, but I read the whole page and it never names Athena. A newcomer who came to learn what Athena is leaves without an answer, and nothing explains why a page about a different project is here.
findings.source: <title>How firstmate handles work</title>; the first heading is "How firstmate handles work"

findings.text: The page assumes the reader already knows what "the study" is and who made it. It never says that the study is the product being shown, or that this page is an example of what that product makes.
findings.source: "A reading of firstmate at one pinned commit, from the study firstmate-work-handling."

findings.text: This explains how firstmate works but not what it is for. It doesn't say who uses it or that the workers are AI coding agents. A reader has to piece that together from terms like "harness" and "captain".
findings.source: Start here > What firstmate is: "Firstmate takes an item from a backlog and gives it to a worker, which does the work in its own isolated worktree"

findings.text: The person who approves merges is never explained. The page admits this gap instead of filling it, so a newcomer can't picture who is actually involved.
findings.source: Glossary > captain: "The text says no more about who the captain is."

findings.text: The numbered walk-through of one task is clear and concrete. It is the strongest part of the page for a reader who already cares about firstmate.
findings.source: Start here > One piece of work, start to finish

findings.text: Internal schema terms leak into the page here, and the passage is hard for an outsider to read.
findings.source: Limits of this study > f2: "A guard of none has no value in guard_evaluated_by for nobody."

findings.text: There is no next step anywhere on the page. It gives no link to Athena, no way to install or run anything, and no link to firstmate except a bare git URL in the header. The claim sources are file:line strings, not links to those files.
